evals.prompt: Using the dx-resilience tools, assess Layer-3 failover coverage for two redundant VIFs. VIF-A advertises 10.10.0.0/24, 10.10.1.0/24, 10.10.2.0/24, 10.10.3.0/24. VIF-B advertises the same four prefixes. Will all prefixes survive a single VIF failure?
evals.expected_output: Reports full symmetric coverage: 0 gaps, all four prefixes covered on both VIFs. If either VIF fails, the peer covers 100% of the prefixes. No failover risk in this direction.
assertions: reports zero gaps
states all prefixes are covered on both VIFs
does not invent a gap where prefix sets are identical

evals.prompt: Assess DX failover coverage. VIF-A advertises 10.10.0.0/24, 10.10.1.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24. VIF-B advertises 10.10.0.0/24, 10.10.1.0/24. What is at risk?
evals.expected_output: Flags 192.168.1.0/24 as a hard gap present only on VIF-A. If VIF-A fails, traffic to 192.168.1.0/24 is blackholed because VIF-B has no coverage for it. The two 10.10 prefixes are covered.
assertions: identifies 192.168.1.0/24 as a gap present only on VIF-A
states the blackhole consequence if VIF-A fails
does not flag the shared 10.10 prefixes as gaps

evals.prompt: Assess DX failover coverage. VIF-A advertises 10.10.0.0/22. VIF-B advertises 10.10.0.0/22 and 10.10.1.0/24. Is 10.10.1.0/24 at risk if VIF-B fails?
evals.expected_output: No gap. 10.10.1.0/24 on VIF-B is fully covered by VIF-A's 10.10.0.0/22 supernet, and the /22 is present on both. Coverage is CIDR-aware, so a more-specific prefix is covered by a peer's containing supernet.
assertions: states 10.10.1.0/24 is covered by the 10.10.0.0/22 supernet
reports zero gaps
does not treat the more-specific prefix as missing

evals.prompt: Assess DX failover coverage. VIF-A advertises only 10.10.1.0/24. VIF-B advertises 10.10.0.0/22. If VIF-B fails, what part of the /22 is at risk?
evals.expected_output: Partial supernet coverage. VIF-A covers only 10.10.1.0/24 of VIF-B's 10.10.0.0/22; the uncovered residual is 10.10.0.0/24 and 10.10.2.0/23 — reachable while VIF-B is up, blackholed if it fails. Conditional severity: confirm whether workloads exist in the residual ranges.
assertions: identifies the uncovered residual as 10.10.0.0/24 and 10.10.2.0/23
does not call the /22 fully covered
asks whether workloads exist in the residual ranges (conditional severity)

evals.prompt: Assess DX failover coverage. VIF-A advertises 10.10.0.0/24, 10.10.1.0/24, 10.10.2.0/23. VIF-B advertises 10.10.0.0/22. Is the /22 fully protected if VIF-B fails?
evals.expected_output: Fully covered. VIF-A's three more-specifics (10.10.0.0/24 + 10.10.1.0/24 + 10.10.2.0/23) exactly tile VIF-B's 10.10.0.0/22, so every address is reachable via VIF-A. Zero gaps, no partial-supernet — the residual is empty.
assertions: states the /22 is fully covered because the more-specifics tile it
reports zero gaps and zero partial-supernet
does not report a false partial or gap for the tiled supernet

evals.prompt: VIF-A and VIF-B both advertise 10.10.0.0/24 and 10.10.1.0/24 over Direct Connect, but VIF-A prepends its AS-path so VIF-B is preferred. Is the AS-path difference a failover coverage gap?
evals.expected_output: No. Coverage is by prefix presence; both prefixes exist on both VIFs, so there is full coverage. Differing AS-path/MED/communities are intentional traffic engineering, not a failover gap.
assertions: states there is full coverage / zero gaps
explains AS-path differences are traffic engineering, not a gap
does not flag the prepended prefixes as missing

evals.prompt: When auditing redundant Direct Connect VIFs for failover resilience, which BGP directions must be checked and why?
evals.expected_output: Both directions: accepted (on-prem to AWS) and advertised (AWS to on-prem). A prefix missing in the accepted direction means AWS cannot reach that on-prem destination after failover; missing in the advertised direction means on-prem cannot reach that AWS destination. In multi-DXGW topologies the advertised sets can differ per VIF.
assertions: states both accepted and advertised directions must be checked
explains the failover consequence of a gap in each direction
notes advertised routes can differ per VIF in multi-DXGW setups

evals.prompt: A Direct Connect resilience assessment shows one redundant VIF with BGP up but zero received routes, while its peer shows a full table. Should this be reported as an empty VIF immediately?
evals.expected_output: Not immediately. An empty accepted table on a BGP-up VIF is ambiguous — it may be genuinely empty or the ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes view may not have converged yet (eventually-consistent, can lag minutes). Recommend re-running to confirm before asserting an empty-VIF finding; treat as point-in-time.
assertions: cautions that an empty view on a BGP-up VIF may be propagation lag, not a true empty VIF
recommends re-running / confirming before asserting the finding

evals.prompt: Is there an official AWS API that returns the BGP-received routes for a private Direct Connect virtual interface, or is that impossible?
evals.expected_output: Yes — ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes returns the routes for a virtual interface (accepted and advertised directions), including private VIFs. Does not claim the capability is impossible or fabricate an alternative.
assertions: identifies ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes as the API that returns VIF routes
does not claim received routes for private VIFs cannot be retrieved
does not fabricate a nonexistent API or workaround
